concept_mcqs.stem:
You’re reviewing a low‑fi wireframe prototype with the following navigation map and back-button settings:

```text
Frames:
A: Product list
B: Product details
C: Cart
D: Checkout – Shipping
E: Checkout – Payment
F: Order confirmation

Transitions:
A -> B  (Tap product)
B -> C  (Tap “Add to cart”)
C -> D  (Tap “Checkout”)
D -> E  (Tap “Continue”)
E -> F  (Tap “Pay”)

Back actions:
B (Back): Back to previous
C (Back): Navigate to A (hard link)
D (Back): Navigate to C (hard link)
E (Back): Back to previous
```

A user lands on B via a deep link (they never visited A), then proceeds B → C → D → E. On E they tap the back icon twice quickly. Where do they land after the two taps, and what subtle modeling issue does this reveal?
options: They land on D; mixing soft back with hard links causes no issue because history is linear here.
They land on A; two backs always take the user to the start of the flow regardless of how they arrived.
They remain on E; rapid taps are debounced and only one back action will fire.
They land on C; mixing stack-pop (Back to previous) with hard links creates an artificial history that won’t match real OS back behavior.
concept_mcqs.explanation: First back from E uses “Back to previous” → D. Second back on D is a hard link → C. So they land on C. Because C’s and D’s backs are hard links, the prototype manufactures a path that may not reflect an OS back stack (e.g., a true back on D would return to E if it had been reached via an intercept). Mixing back-to-previous with hard links drifts from realistic stack behavior.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Feels plausible because history looks linear, but the mix of back types does matter. C: Sounds like a common misconception that back rewinds to origin; not how a stack works. D: Figma doesn’t debounce back actions by default; two taps can execute two transitions.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A button component is set up in Figma:

```text
Component: Button / Primary
Auto layout: Horizontal, spacing=8, padding=12/16
Layers (left→right): [Icon-16] [Label]
Icon layer: 16×16, visibility controlled by boolean property `icon`
Label: Auto width
Button resizing (inside parent): Fill container (width)
Problem: When `icon=false`, icon is hidden but 8px left gap remains before the label in instances.
```

What change best guarantees there’s no leftover gap when the icon is off, across all instances and sizes?
options: Wrap [Icon-16] and [Label] in a nested auto‑layout frame and use a variant where left padding is reduced by 8px when `icon=false`.
Change the label to Fill container so it absorbs the space when the icon is hidden.
Switch the button’s horizontal distribution to Space Between so hidden layers collapse to zero.
Set the frame’s alignment to Left; center alignment causes the phantom gap.
concept_mcqs.explanation: When a layer is hidden, spacing between items remains. Tying padding to a variant (icon on/off) removes the extra left gap reliably. Space Between doesn’t collapse spacing; label Fill doesn’t remove inter‑item spacing; changing alignment doesn’t address spacing persistence.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Tempting because Space Between redistributes space, but it doesn’t eliminate inter‑item spacing with hidden layers. C: Common attempt to soak space, but spacing is between items, not inside the label. D: Alignment changes positioning, not inter‑item spacing.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A desktop UI kit specifies both a spacing grid and a typographic baseline:

```text
Layout spacing scale: 8px steps (8, 16, 24, 32, ...)
Typography baseline: 4px grid

Spec excerpt
- Card internal padding: 24
- Body text line-height: 20
- Spacing between components: 12
- Primary button height: 36
```

Which single measurement is off-spec for inter-component spacing and will create ragged vertical rhythm between components?
options: Card internal padding: 24
Primary button height: 36
Spacing between components: 12
Body text line-height: 20
concept_mcqs.explanation: Inter-component spacing is defined on the 8px scale, so 12px breaks the layout rhythm. A 20px line-height and 36px control height both sit on the 4px baseline and are acceptable for type and control metrics. Padding 24 is on the 8px spacing scale.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: 24 is a multiple of 8, so it’s fine. B: 20 isn’t on the 8px scale, but line-heights follow the 4px baseline, not the spacing scale. D: 36 breaks 8px but aligns to the 4px baseline, which is acceptable for controls.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You need two equal-width cards on a 360px-wide mobile artboard using this grid:

```text
Columns: 4
Gutter: 8
Outer margins: 16
```

Each card spans exactly 2 columns. What width should each card be to sit perfectly on the grid?
options: 172px
160px
168px
152px
concept_mcqs.explanation: Content width = 360 − (2×16 margins) − (3×8 gutters) = 360 − 32 − 24 = 304. One column = 304/4 = 76. A 2‑column span includes one gutter: 2×76 + 8 = 160.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: 152 ignores the included gutter within a 2‑column span. C/D: Overestimates by adding extra gutters or ignoring margins.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A modal in your wireframe prototype is configured as follows:

```text
Trigger: Tap “Filter”
Action: Open overlay → Modal/Filters
Overlay position: Center
Background: Dimmed (40%)
Close when clicking outside: Disabled
‘Esc’ key closes: Enabled
Modal has a Close (X) button wired to Close overlay
```

During a usability review on desktop, users click outside the modal and nothing happens. What is the most accurate fix to reflect expected desktop behavior without compromising mobile behavior (where accidental dismiss is risky)?
options: Enable “Close when clicking outside” and remove the Close (X) button to reduce duplicate affordances.
Enable outside click and increase the background dim to 60% to make the intent clearer.
Create a desktop variant of the overlay with outside click enabled, and keep the mobile variant with it disabled; swap variants by breakpoint.
Keep outside click disabled; add a second Close (X) in the modal footer for redundancy.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Desktop patterns commonly allow clicking the backdrop to dismiss, while mobile often avoids accidental dismissals. Using variants by breakpoint models the differing expectations accurately.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Removing the Close (X) reduces explicit affordance and doesn’t address platform differences. B: Adds clutter without solving the mismatch. D: Dim level doesn’t change dismissal behavior; enabling outside click globally hurts mobile.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You are modeling form validation logic at low fidelity. Current prototype wiring:

```text
Screen: Payment
Elements: [Card #] [Expiry] [CVV] [Name] [Pay button]
States:
S0: Empty (Pay disabled)
S1: Some invalid input (Pay enabled by mistake)
S2: All valid (Pay enabled)
Serr: Error from gateway (inline error under Pay)

Current issue: In S1, tapping Pay navigates to Confirmation due to a hard link on the button.
```

What change best communicates the intended interaction without code, and prevents the erroneous navigation in S1?
options: Link Pay in S1 to a toast overlay saying “Invalid fields”, but still allow proceeding to Confirmation after dismissing the toast.
Use two Pay button variants (enabled/disabled). In S1 show the disabled variant with no interaction; only S2’s enabled variant links to Confirmation.
Keep the hard link but add an intermediate “Validating…” screen before Confirmation to imply a check.
Replace the Pay interaction with a sticky note that says “Validate here” and remove the link.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Variant gating makes the prototype behave correctly: disabled has no interaction, enabled proceeds. This communicates logic through interaction rather than annotation or leaky flows.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Non-interactive notes don’t demonstrate behavior. C: Still allows invalid progression and implies server-side only checks. D: Still proceeds on invalid input, normalizing a broken path.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Your design system is defining color tokens. Two proposals are on the table:

```text
Proposal 1 (brand-first):
- brand/blue-500, brand/blue-600
- brand/green-500, brand/green-600
- text/on-dark, text/on-light
- button/primary/bg → brand/blue-600
- button/primary/text → text/on-dark

Proposal 2 (semantic-first):
- action/primary/bg
- action/primary/text
- action/secondary/bg
- action/secondary/text
- surface/default
- text/high, text/medium
- theme/brand/blue-600 (alias)
- action/primary/bg → alias(theme/brand/blue-600)
```

You must add a “warning” emphasis next quarter and support a seasonal theme. Which proposal better scales, and why?
options: Both are equivalent if you document a mapping table in the README.
Proposal 1; brand hues are already listed so adding warning is just another color.
Proposal 1; it’s closer to developer variables that often use raw colors.
Proposal 2; semantic tokens allow new emphases and themes by re-aliasing without renaming component references.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Semantic tokens decouple meaning from brand. New emphases (warning) and themes can be supported by pointing semantic tokens to new brand aliases without refactoring components.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Adding raw colors doesn’t propagate meaning or handle themes cleanly. C: Developer familiarity doesn’t solve scalability. D: Documentation cannot offset hard-coded brand dependencies.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You’re converting a card to be responsive in Figma. Requirements: the hero image must keep a 16:9 ratio as the card width changes. Current setup:

```text
Card: Auto layout (Vertical), padding 16, gap 12
Image layer: 640×360 placed inside a frame
Image fill: Image (Crop)
Image layer resizing: Fill container (width), Fixed height (360)
```

When the card width shrinks, the image distorts or crops awkwardly. What change preserves 16:9 without manual overrides?
options: Wrap the image in its own frame sized by auto layout, and set that wrapper frame’s constraints to Scale; then resize the wrapper proportionally from the card.
Use Space Between in the card’s auto layout so the image keeps its space.
Set the image layer to Fill container for both width and height; Figma will keep the aspect ratio automatically.
Switch the card from Auto layout to a fixed-size group so children don’t resize.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Placing the image inside a wrapper that scales preserves its aspect as the wrapper resizes proportionally with the card. Fill container + fixed height distorts; groups/fixed sizes break responsiveness; Space Between affects gaps, not aspect ratio.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Fill both axes forces stretching; aspect isn’t preserved. C: Freezes layout, losing responsiveness. D: Misapplies distribution to a sizing problem.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You’re laying out filter chips in a responsive toolbar.

```text
Toolbar frame: Auto layout (Horizontal)
Wrap: Enabled
Gap between items: 8
Padding: 12/16
Chip: Auto width, min width 64, horizontal padding 12
```

As the toolbar width changes, rows wrap but spacing within each row becomes visually uneven. Which configuration yields the most consistent row appearance across widths?
options: Keep Left alignment with a fixed 8px gap; let wrap handle line breaks naturally.
Center align the row so the ragged right edge is balanced.
Increase the gap to 12 so it divides evenly into more widths.
Set horizontal distribution to Space Between so chips expand to fill each row evenly.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Left alignment with a fixed gap yields predictable, even intra-row spacing. Space Between redistributes gaps unevenly per row. Arbitrary gap increases don’t solve unevenness; centering emphasizes ragged edges.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Common but causes variable intra-row spacing. C: Numerology doesn’t align with available widths. D: Centering may look tidy but doesn’t address spacing consistency.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You’re testing a responsive header in Figma. Current constraints:

```text
Header frame width: resizes
Logo: Constraints → Left & Right
Left action (☰): Constraints → Left
Right action (🔍): Constraints → Right
```

On wider screens the logo drifts off-center. What change correctly locks the logo to center across widths while keeping actions pinned to edges?
options: Fix the header width to prevent drift.
Set the logo’s constraints to Center and remove Left & Right.
Set the header to Space Between and let auto layout center the logo between actions.
Group the logo with the left action so they scale together.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Using the Center constraint keeps the logo centered as the header resizes, independent of edge‑pinned actions. Grouping with the left action pulls it off-center; Space Between centers the free space, not necessarily the logo; fixing width defeats responsiveness.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Feels like it keeps relative positions, but ruins centering. C: Space Between aligns outer edges, not a centered middle element. D: Avoids the problem by removing responsiveness.

scenario_questions.scenario:
Your low‑fi wireframes for a 3‑step checkout reveal user confusion in testing. The flow is:

```text
Cart → Shipping → Payment → Confirmation
- Back on Shipping: hard link to Cart
- Back on Payment: back to previous
- "Edit" links on Payment open field-specific overlays (e.g., Change address)
- Errors: gateway decline should keep the user on Payment with an inline message
Test observation: When users deep-link into Payment (promo email) and then tap Back, some end up on Cart unexpectedly. Several try to re-enter details thinking they lost progress.
```
scenario_questions.task: Propose changes to the wireframe structure and interaction logic to make back-navigation and error handling predictable for deep-linked and linear entries alike. Specify exactly which frames change, which links become back-to-previous vs hard links, and how overlays return focus. Justify each choice against the observed confusion.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A solid answer will replace hard links on intermediate steps with back-to-previous so the stack reflects real entry order; ensure Cart is only reached by an explicit "View cart" action; move Edit overlays to modal overlays that close back to Payment and restore focus to the edited field; model Payment errors as an inline message under the Pay button with the form state retained; ensure a consistent breadcrumb or progress indicator that is purely informational (not hard-linked) to avoid jumps. Deep link to Payment should prefill Shipping state and set back-to-previous targeting the entry source (e.g., PDP or email), not Cart. If a user reaches Payment from Shipping, back returns to Shipping; if they deep-link and then open Edit Address, closing returns to Payment, not Cart. Confirmation is only reachable from successful Pay. All back actions should be "back to previous" except where a clear forward-only transition is required; remove hard links that skip steps.

rubric.criterion: Identifies and corrects the hard-link causing unexpected jump to Cart (switch to back-to-previous).
Explains deep-link handling: establishes a valid history stack and preserves form state on return.
Specifies overlay behavior: close returns focus to invoking control/field on Payment; no unintended navigation.
Models error handling: inline message on Payment with state retention and no navigation on error.

scenario_questions.scenario:
You must convert mobile wireframes of a content feed into high‑fidelity screens for mobile and tablet. Constraints:

```text
Content density: 6–10 cards per view on tablet, 3–5 on mobile
Text: Title, metadata line, 2 lines body
Media: 16:9 thumbnail per card
Grid proposals:
- Mobile: 4 cols, 16 margins, 8 gutters
- Tablet: 8 cols, 24 margins, 12 gutters
Type ramp candidates:
- A: Title 18/24, Meta 12/16, Body 14/20
- B: Title 20/28, Meta 12/18, Body 16/24
```
Testing shows truncation on mobile titles and overly airy tablet layouts.
scenario_questions.task: Select a grid and type ramp combination and describe exact column spans, paddings, and line-heights to hit the density targets without truncation beyond 2 lines on mobile. Explain how you’ll enforce a consistent 8px spacing scale and 4px baseline across both breakpoints, and how the 16:9 media will be maintained without manual overrides.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Choose the given 4/8 column grids. For mobile: two-across cards at 2-column spans (width = 2 col + 1 gutter), padding 16, gap 8, title 18/24 (2 lines max), body 14/20. For tablet: 3-across at 2- or 3-column spans depending on target density, padding 20–24, gap 12; type ramp B for tablet titles (20/28) to use space while keeping 2‑line cap. Use 8px spacing scale for inter-card spacing; 4px baseline for line-heights (20, 24, 28, etc.). Maintain 16:9 via nested frame with Scale constraints or component with fixed aspect wrapper; set image to Fill width inside wrapper. Provide explicit spans (e.g., tablet card spans 2 cols for 4-up or 3 cols for 3-up) to hit density. Justify choices against truncation and density observations.

rubric.criterion: Chooses appropriate type ramp per breakpoint and justifies against truncation/airiness.
Specifies precise column spans, paddings, gaps consistent with given grids.
Explains baseline (4px) and spacing (8px) enforcement across components.
Details a robust method to maintain 16:9 media responsively (wrapper + constraints).

scenario_questions.scenario:
A new design system must support theming and growing component complexity. Current draft shows buttons built directly with brand tokens and ad‑hoc states:

```text
Button Primary (light theme)
- Background: #1463FF
- Text: #FFFFFF
- Hover: #2A75FF
- Pressed: #0F4ED1
- Disabled: #9CB9FF @ 40% opacity
Variants: size (sm/md/lg) only
```

Roadmap: add Secondary and Destructive emphases; add dark theme; ship i18n with long labels.
scenario_questions.task: Propose a token and component variant structure that scales. Specify semantic tokens and their aliasing to brand tokens, state mapping (default/hover/pressed/disabled), size variants, icon boolean, and how you’ll avoid opacity hacks for disabled. Explain how this structure reduces overrides when themes or emphases are added.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Define semantic tokens (action/primary/bg, action/primary/text, action/primary/bg/hover, /pressed, /disabled/bg, /disabled/text). Alias them to brand for each theme (theme/light/brand/blue-600, etc.). Build button variants with properties: emphasis (primary/secondary/destructive), size (sm/md/lg), icon (boolean), state (interactive variants or prototyping states). Disabled uses dedicated semantic tokens (e.g., action/primary/disabled/bg) not opacity of active colors to preserve contrast and consistency across themes. Sizes set paddings and min heights; icon boolean adjusts padding/spacing without leftover gaps. Result: adding new themes only re-aliases tokens; adding emphases adds a new semantic set without refactoring components.

rubric.criterion: Defines a clear semantic token set and explains aliasing to theme/brand tokens.
Maps states without opacity hacks; provides disabled-specific tokens.
Specifies component variant properties (emphasis, size, icon, state) and their effects on spacing.
Explains how the approach minimizes overrides when adding themes/emphases/i18n.

scenario_questions.scenario:
In a click‑through prototype of a search flow, users fail to notice the primary action on mobile. Current high‑fi:

```text
Header: 16px margins
Results list: cards with Title 18/24, Body 14/20
Primary CTA: “Save search” as a ghost button at top-right of results
Accent color: Blue 600 for CTAs; Blue 500 on hover
Secondary CTA: “Create alert” as text link at bottom
```

Observation: Participants scroll past the header quickly and never use the primary CTA. They do tap "Create alert" often.
scenario_questions.task: Recommend changes to typography, color usage, grid placement, and component treatment to fix the affordance issue without adding more elements. Justify how each change will alter attention and tap behavior on mobile.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Move the primary CTA into a sticky footer action area or pin it at the end of the first viewport using the grid (full-width or aligned to column span) so it’s in the scroll path. Switch from ghost to filled primary (action/primary/bg) to increase contrast. Adjust type hierarchy so card titles don’t overpower the CTA: keep Title 18/24 but set CTA label to 16/24 with medium weight and ensure 44px min hit target. Maintain 16px outer margins; use 8px gaps. Consider in-card inline CTA if it aligns with task. Ensure secondary link uses secondary token, not primary blue, to reduce competition. Result: primary CTA becomes visible and touchable at first scroll stop; secondary is visually subordinate.

rubric.criterion: Repositions primary CTA using the grid to where it will be encountered (e.g., sticky/footer or first viewport end).
Improves CTA visual prominence via filled style and correct tokens vs ghost/text.
Adjusts typography and hit-area to improve tapability without harming content hierarchy.
Explains expected behavior change grounded in attention flow on mobile.

practical_tasks.title: Low‑fidelity wireframe prototype: 3‑step checkout with edge cases
practical_tasks.brief: Produce a clickable low‑fidelity prototype that models the complete checkout flow with realistic interaction logic, including deep-link entry and error handling. Keep visuals to wires and greys; focus on layout and logic.
acceptance_criteria: Frames for: Cart, Shipping, Payment, Confirmation, and necessary overlays (Edit address, 3DS challenge, Error).
Back navigation modeled with back-to-previous (no hard links that skip steps).
Primary actions disabled until prerequisites met; enabled states only link forward.
Error paths modeled: declined payment stays on Payment with inline error; 3DS opens overlay and returns to Payment on success/failure.
Deep-link entry to Payment modeled; back from Payment returns to true previous, not Cart, when deep-linked.
Clickable prototype link with sharing enabled; all hotspots labeled; page and frames named consistently.

rubric.criterion: Flow completeness: all required screens and overlays present and reachable.
Interaction logic: correct gating of actions, realistic back behavior, no leaky success on invalid states.
Error/deep-link handling: inline error behavior and deep-link back path modeled accurately.
Organization and clarity: consistent naming, labeled hotspots, clean wire visuals focused on structure.

practical_tasks.title: High‑fidelity UI screens: responsive checkout (mobile + desktop) with systemized components
practical_tasks.brief: Design high‑fidelity screens for the same checkout, using a grid, type ramp, color tokens, and reusable components. Deliver mobile and desktop breakpoints showing key states.
acceptance_criteria: Two breakpoints delivered: mobile (e.g., 360×640) and desktop (e.g., 1440×900).
Grids applied: declare columns, gutters, and margins for both breakpoints; elements align to grid.
Typography uses a consistent ramp with 4px baseline-aligned line-heights; body copy <= 2 lines where specified.
Buttons, inputs, and alerts built as components with variants (size, emphasis, state, icon boolean) and Auto Layout; no manual per-instance spacing fixes.
Color tokens used semantically (e.g., action/primary/bg) and aliased to brand colors; no hard-coded hex in components.
Images maintain 16:9 aspect via wrappers; hit targets meet 44px minimum on mobile.
Export or prototype link showing default, error, and success states for Payment; annotation or inspectable tokens page included.

rubric.criterion: Grid and alignment: correct, consistent application across both breakpoints.
Typography: coherent ramp, baseline alignment, and readable measures without unintended truncation.
Components and variants: reusable, tokenized, with correct Auto Layout behavior and states.
Tokens and theming: semantic tokens and aliasing used; no hard-coded styling in instances.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You ran two rounds of usability testing on the same interactive prototype with different labels. Excerpt of your task data for Task 2 ("Change your plan"):
```text
Round 1 (n=10)
- Nav labels: Home, Plans, Billing, Support
- Success rate: 40%
- First-click on "Plans": 20%
- First-click on "Billing": 60%
- Median time-to-first-meaningful-click: 19s
- Notes: 7/10 said they were looking for "subscription".

Change between rounds: Renamed "Plans" to "Subscriptions". No layout changes.

Round 2 (n=10)
- Nav labels: Home, Subscriptions, Billing, Support
- Success rate: 75%
- First-click on "Subscriptions": 70%
- First-click on "Billing": 20%
- Misroutes that still succeed via "Billing": 4/10
- Median time-to-first-meaningful-click: 8s
```
Given this, what is the most defensible next iteration to address the remaining misroutes without adding new nav items?
options: Add a tooltip on hover over "Billing" that explains plan management is under Subscriptions.
Revert the rename back to "Plans" and move it to the first position in the nav for higher salience.
Increase the visual weight (bold + primary color) of "Subscriptions" in the nav to overpower "Billing".
Add a lightweight cross-link on the Billing landing page: "Looking to manage or cancel a plan? Go to Subscriptions" as the first element above the fold.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The rename improved first-click success and time-to-click, indicating label match. The residual misroutes start on Billing, which is still a plausible entry point. A contextual cross-link on the Billing page preserves the improved IA while rescuing misroutes with minimal change, likely converting those 4/10 faster without creating new confusion.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B is tempting because prominence can increase clicks, but Round 2 shows label match, not position, is the driver; moving it may disrupt other tasks. C sounds helpful but hover tooltips don’t exist on touch and are unreliable/annoying even on desktop. D tweaks visual weight but doesn’t help users who already clicked into Billing; it also risks harming overall nav balance.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A modal overlay in your Figma prototype won’t scroll on mobile during tests. Inspect of the prototype connection and frame:
```text
Prototype connection
- Trigger: On click (Open overlay)
- Position: Center
- Close when clicking outside: On
- Add background behind overlay: 20% blur
- No scroll through: On
- While overlay open: Prevent interaction with background: Off

Overlay frame
- Auto layout: Vertical
- Clip content: On
- Scrolling: None
- Height: 520 px (content can exceed)
```
What change will most likely allow users to scroll overlay content while keeping background locked?
options: Set the overlay frame to Scrolling: Vertical and turn Clip content Off so overflow content becomes scrollable within the overlay.
Turn "No scroll through" Off so the page behind can scroll, which users can use to reach more content.
Switch overlay Position to Manual and enable "Fix position when scrolling" on the overlay.
Replace the overlay interaction with "Open link in new page" so the modal becomes a full screen that naturally scrolls.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The overlay frame itself is non-scrollable (Scrolling: None) and clips overflow, so content cannot scroll. Making the frame vertically scrollable and allowing overflow to render within it enables scrolling while keeping the background locked via "No scroll through: On".
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A changes position behavior but not scrollability. B re-enables background scroll, which fails the modal pattern and confuses users. D changes the UX to a new page, invalidating your modal test and potentially altering task performance.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You are validating text color choices against WCAG AA. Export from your contrast checker:
```csv
pair,label,foreground,background,contrast_ratio,sample_text_size_px
1,Primary on White,#1E62F0,#FFFFFF,4.3,14
2,Slate on White,#4A5568,#FFFFFF,5.4,14
3,Muted on Warm Grey,#7A7A7A,#F5F2EE,3.8,14
4,Primary on Off-Black,#1E62F0,#0E0E10,7.8,14
```
For 14px normal body text, which pair can you keep as-is for AA compliance?
options: Keep pairs 2 and 4.
Keep pairs 1 and 3.
Keep pair 2 only.
Keep pair 1 only.
concept_mcqs.explanation: WCAG AA requires at least 4.5:1 for normal text at 14px. Pair 2 is 5.4:1 and pair 4 is 7.8:1, so both pass. Pair 1 is 4.3 (fails), pair 3 is 3.8 (fails).
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A is close but 4.3 is below the 4.5 threshold. B ignores that pair 4 massively exceeds the minimum. D includes two failing ratios, which might tempt if you misremember the threshold as 4.0 or assume off-black backgrounds relax it (they do not).

concept_mcqs.explanation: Separating inline (left/right) and block (top/bottom) padding makes the intent explicit and maps cleanly to platform properties. Using semantically named global tokens and aliasing them in a component token reduces ambiguity across layouts.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A still hides directionality in a single value. C hard-codes a shorthand string that may not translate across platforms or into token-aware tooling. D leaves vertical ambiguous with "auto", which is not implementable as a token value.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You are rewriting a task in your unmoderated test plan. Current wording:
```text
"Find the nearest clinic and book an appointment in under 2 minutes."
```
Which rewrite best reduces bias and still yields a measurable outcome?
options:
"Find the nearest clinic and book an appointment."

Separate timing is measured by the platform, not stated in the prompt.

"Find any clinic and tell us how long you think it would take to book."

Relies on self-reported time to reduce pressure.

"Prove you can book in under 2 minutes by following the fastest route."

Motivates performance via competitive framing.

"Use the map to find the nearest clinic and try to book quickly."

Gives a hint to aid discoverability and encourages speed.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Removing the time constraint from the prompt avoids demand characteristics while still allowing precise timing via instrumentation. This preserves comparability of measured time without nudging behavior.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B injects a hint (map) that biases path choice. C creates performance pressure and primes speed over natural behavior. D replaces objective timing with unreliable self-report.

concept_mcqs.stem:
First-click data for the task "Cancel your subscription" on your prototype nav:
```text
Nav items: Home, Subscriptions, Billing, Help
First-click distribution (n=30):
- Subscriptions: 33%
- Billing: 50%
- Help: 13%
- Home: 4%
Qual notes: "Cancel" perceived as a billing action; some expect it under plan management.
```
Without adding new nav items, which change most likely improves first-click success?
options: Add a confirmation page after cancel to reassure users they've completed the task.
Rename "Billing" to "Billing & Subscriptions" to acknowledge management actions live there.
Rename "Billing" to "Billing & Payments" and keep "Subscriptions" as-is.
Move "Subscriptions" to first position in the nav to increase salience for the task.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Data shows most users click Billing first and associate cancelation with it. Making that label explicitly include Subscriptions aligns with their mental model and should increase correct first clicks without adding nav items.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A keeps the ambiguity between billing and subscription management. C changes position but not the underlying label mismatch. D is post-action reassurance; it doesn’t change first-click behavior.

concept_mcqs.stem:
A dev shipped icon buttons at 36×36 px because the Figma handoff only showed the visible frame size. Inspect excerpt:
```text
Component: IconButton / Primary
Frame size: 36 × 36 px
Auto layout: Centered
Padding: 8 px all sides
Notes: —
```
Which addition to the handoff most reliably prevents this issue across platforms?
options: Link to Apple HIG and Material docs about 44–48 px targets and trust devs to apply it.
Annotate the frame with a 44 × 44 px redline and a note: "Min touch area 44 px".
Define and reference a token in the component docs, e.g., `size.touchTarget.min = 44dp` and include it in the Inspect panel via a property.
Embed a prototype hotspot that is 44 × 44 px to simulate the hit area during testing.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Encoding the requirement as a named token and referencing it in the component ensures it survives platform translation and shows up in Inspect/handoff tools. It’s actionable and enforceable.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A is easy to miss and not machine-readable. C is generic guidance, not a spec. D helps in testing but doesn’t carry through to implementation semantics.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Testers were able to click a disabled CTA in your interactive component. Variant setup excerpt:
```text
Component: Button
Variants (properties): state = {enabled, disabled}; emphasis = {primary, secondary}
Prototype connections: Node "Label" (inside Button) has On Click → Navigate to Checkout.
All variants share the same Label node.
```
What is the minimal wiring change to prevent activation of the disabled state without altering visuals?
options: Move the navigation interaction to the component set level so it applies only when state=enabled.
Disable "Include in Interaction" for the Label node in disabled variants; leave enabled variants unchanged.
Add an invisible overlay on top of the disabled variant to block clicks while leaving interactions as-is.
Remove the On Click interaction from the Label and add it only to the Button frame in the enabled variants.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Interactions in Figma are attached to specific nodes and carry across variants if shared. By moving the interaction to the Button frame and scoping it to enabled variants, disabled variants won’t inherit it, preventing activation.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B obscures the issue and complicates hit areas. C sounds right, but Figma doesn’t offer per-variant "Include in Interaction" toggles for a shared node without splitting it; the reliable pattern is scoping interactions to enabled variants. D doesn’t exist as a conditional at the set level; interactions are per-node/variant.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You are preparing a portfolio case. Metrics collected around your redesign:
```text
Before (4 weeks):
- Signup completion: 42% (n=12,400 sessions)
- Mobile share: 70%
- Promo campaign: None

After (4 weeks):
- Signup completion: 54% (n=18,900 sessions)
- Mobile share: 78%
- Promo campaign: Running (20% discount)
- Control geo (no redesign): 44% → 46%
```
Which analytic framing best supports a credible causal story in your case study?
options: Aggregate 8 weeks before/after to smooth noise and report the overall lift.
Show the 12-point increase as a headline and attribute it to the redesign with selected user quotes.
Use a difference-in-differences view comparing the redesigned geo vs control over time, and discuss the promo as a confound.
Normalize by mobile share and report a mobile-only conversion increase.
concept_mcqs.explanation: A difference-in-differences comparison with a control segment strengthens causal claims and explicitly acknowledges concurrent confounds like the promo, making your story credible.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A over-attributes and cherry-picks. C addresses mix shift but ignores the promo and time trends. D smooths but still lacks a control and ignores confounds.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Your unmoderated test has high drop-off on the first screen. Current intro and consent:
```text
Welcome to our study! Please read this 3-page consent carefully. Keep this tab open.
You must think aloud at all times. If you stop speaking, the session will be terminated.
Tasks (8 total) will take ~25–30 minutes. Click Start to enable camera, mic, and screen.
```
Which change is most likely to reduce attrition without biasing behavior?
options: Add more reassurance copy about privacy across all task screens.
Shorten and plain-language the consent into a single screen, get permissions inline after a 30-second practice task, and keep tasks to 4–5 focused flows.
Increase incentive size to compensate for effort and keep the flow unchanged.
Replace think-aloud with a mandatory post-task survey to shorten tasks.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Reducing cognitive load and front-loaded friction (long consent, immediate permissions) and trimming task count reduces attrition while preserving natural behavior. A short practice also sets expectations without biasing task performance.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A changes the method and loses rich behavioral data. C masks the UX problem instead of fixing it. D is helpful tone-wise but doesn’t materially reduce the barriers causing early exits.

scenario_questions.scenario:
You tested an interactive checkout prototype (mobile) with 8 participants. Key findings excerpt:
```text
Task: Apply a promo code and check total.
- 6/8 attempted to type the code into the "Notes" field on the Cart.
- The promo input lives on the Payment step as a small link: "Have a code?"
- Time-to-discovery of "Have a code?": median 42s; 3/8 never found it.
- 2/8 tapped back when the keyboard covered the total; they thought the promo didn’t apply.
- Error message after invalid code is inline, 12px gray text below input.
```
Constraints: must keep a two-step checkout (Cart → Payment). You own the prototype and the next test plan; devs will not build anything until after your next round.
scenario_questions.task: Propose specific prototype and content changes to address the issues, and define a focused follow-up usability test plan (participants, tasks, success metrics and thresholds) to validate them. Justify why your changes target the observed failures without introducing new ones.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A strong answer specifies: moving promo entry affordance closer to where users expect it (Cart) or increasing prominence at Payment; elevating "Have a code?" to a button or field with clear label; ensuring the promo input is visible without scrolling and not obscured by the keyboard (use safe area / sticky summary); revising error styles to meet contrast and hierarchy; showing applied promo feedback adjacent to the total with a delta and removable chip. Follow-up test plan: 5–8 participants, mobile, task to apply code and verify total; success defined as first-click on the correct affordance within ~10s, success rate ≥80%, time-to-complete median under ~30–40s, zero participants misusing Notes, all can see updated total without dismissing keyboard; include a negative test (invalid code) to observe error legibility; instrument first-click, time, and path; compare against prior round. Justification ties each change to a specific failure mode (discoverability, placement, visibility under keyboard) and calls out how sticky order summary prevents misinterpretation. Mentions WCAG AA for error contrast.

rubric.criterion: Concrete prototype changes address discoverability (placement/label/prominence) and visibility under keyboard
Error handling and feedback design (contrast, inline placement, removable state) is specified
Follow-up test plan includes participants, tasks, metrics with explicit pass thresholds
Clear justification mapping each change to an observed failure; risks/side-effects considered

scenario_questions.scenario:
Your accessibility review of the account settings prototype found these issues:
```text
- Focus indicator on primary buttons is a 1px low-contrast outline; fails non-text contrast.
- Keyboard trap inside country dropdown (custom menu) when opened in a modal.
- Empty placeholder icons used instead of text labels in the bottom tab bar.
- Success toast auto-dismisses in 2s with important content ("Email changed").
```
You will not write code, but you control the design system specs and handoff package.
scenario_questions.task: Specify the design and system-level changes you will make so these issues are unlikely to recur. Reference the relevant WCAG criteria and describe what you will annotate or tokenize for the handoff so engineers can implement unambiguously.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Propose system-level tokens/specs: focus style token with ≥3:1 contrast against adjacent colors and ≥2px or dual-outline focus ring; WCAG 2.1 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast. For custom dropdowns in modals, spec focus management: on open, focus first selected/active option; Escape/Outside click close; Tab/Shift+Tab cycle within modal (focus trap with sentinel elements); on close, return focus to trigger; WCAG 2.1.2 Keyboard, 2.4.3 Focus Order. Replace unlabeled icons in navigation with visible labels or accessible names in spec; ensure designers provide text labels; WCAG 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions and 1.3.1 Info and Relationships. For toasts with critical updates, require persistent confirmation or at least longer duration with dismiss, and ensure it is not the sole modality (also reflect change in the page state); WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable and 4.1.3 Status Messages. Provide Figma components with annotated behaviors, tokens (e.g., focusRing.color/width/offset), and interaction notes in the component docs; include acceptance criteria in handoff checklist.

rubric.criterion: Maps each issue to a concrete spec/token change usable in handoff (focus, dropdown behavior, labels, toast timing)
Correct WCAG criteria referenced for each issue
Explains how annotations/documentation will make implementation unambiguous
Considers persistence/alternative feedback for status messages and focus return

scenario_questions.scenario:
Engineering reports inconsistent paddings and states across implemented buttons despite a shared component. Current Figma structure excerpt:
```text
Component: Button
Variants: size={sm, md, lg}, emphasis={primary, secondary}
Padding in Inspect: shown as numbers per variant, no tokens referenced.
Focus state: a separate local style, not part of the component set.
```
There’s no centralized token mapping; designers override paddings per variant.
scenario_questions.task: Redesign the handoff so engineers can implement buttons consistently across platforms. Propose a token schema and component spec, including how to expose it in Figma Inspect, and explain how this will prevent drift as the system scales.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Introduce a token schema that separates global and component tokens: e.g., size.scale (sm=32dp, md=40dp, lg=48dp), spacing.inline/block, radius, and state tokens (focusRing.color/width). Button component aliases: `button.padding.inline = {spacing.inline-200}`, `button.padding.block = {spacing.block-200}`, `button.size = {size.scale.md}`, and state variants include focus/hover/pressed within the same component set. In Figma, attach tokens via a plugin or design tokens feature so Inspect shows token names, not just numbers. Document platform mappings (dp/pt) and include an implementation checklist. This prevents drift by removing local numeric overrides and making changes cascade through tokens; variants inherit states uniformly.

rubric.criterion: Token schema proposed (global vs component) with clear aliases and properties relevant to buttons
Component spec includes states within variants and references tokens, not raw numbers
Plan for exposing tokens in Figma Inspect/handoff and cross-platform mapping
Explanation of how the approach prevents future drift

scenario_questions.scenario:
You are assembling a portfolio case for a feature that failed to move its primary KPI but produced strong qualitative wins and several accessibility fixes. You have these assets:
```text
- Pre/post funnel data: +1% (not significant) in completion
- Task data: time-on-task -25% for key flows (n=12 moderated sessions)
- Heuristic + a11y audit: 14 issues → 0 critical, 3 minor remaining
- Before/after prototypes and component updates merged to design system
- Clips of 3 participants praising clarity; 1 participant still confused by copy
- A concurrent promo likely influenced overall traffic quality
```
You want to tell a credible story that still reflects your impact.
scenario_questions.task: Outline the narrative arc and artifact sequence you will use in the case study. Explain how you will present the mixed results ethically and what you will foreground to show value, including how accessibility work and systemization appear in the story.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A strong outline frames the problem and constraints, then the approach (research → prototype → test → iterate), shows the mixed results honestly: limited KPI lift due to confounds, but meaningful efficiency gains (time-on-task), resolved a11y issues (mapped to WCAG), and systemized the fixes into the design system. Sequence: Problem + hypothesis → key usability findings → specific design changes (before/after) → test evidence (task metrics, clips) → a11y audit deltas → system handoff (tokens/components PR) → reflection/next steps. Explicitly note the promo confound and small KPI movement; do not over-claim. Foreground user efficiency, error reduction, and a11y risk mitigation; include links/screens of tokenized focus styles and tap-target updates. Close with what you’d test next to target KPI movement.

rubric.criterion: Clear narrative structure with logical artifact sequence from problem to outcomes
Ethical handling of mixed results and confounds; no over-claiming
Highlights accessibility improvements and their systemization
States next steps or hypotheses to move the primary KPI

practical_tasks.title: Usability Test Report on Interactive Prototype
practical_tasks.brief: Plan and run a small usability evaluation of your interactive prototype focusing on one critical user journey. Iterate the prototype once based on findings and report the results. Use remote moderated or unmoderated methods as appropriate, but the report must make your design decisions and their impact auditable.
acceptance_criteria: Includes a concise objective and hypothesis for the chosen journey.
Provides the test protocol: participant profile, recruitment, task scripts (non-leading), environment, and data to be captured.
Reports raw metrics for each task (success rate, time-on-task, first-click success) and observations; includes at least 5 participants’ data.
Links to or embeds the exact prototype version tested (v1) and the iterated version (v2) with a changelog of what changed and why.
Presents prioritized findings with severity, supporting evidence (timestamps or clips), and maps each to a design change in v2.
Shows before/after evidence of impact on at least two metrics, with a short analysis of learnability vs discoverability effects.
Includes at least one accessibility consideration observed and how it was addressed in v2 (e.g., contrast, target sizes, focus order).
Ends with a decision: ship, iterate again, or pivot, with explicit success thresholds for a next round.

rubric.criterion: Clear objective, hypothesis, and non-leading tasks (auditable protocol)
Complete, credible data (≥5 participants) with core metrics and observations
Traceable prototype iteration (v1→v2) with rationale and changelog
Findings prioritized with severity and evidenced; metric deltas analyzed
Accessibility consideration identified and addressed

practical_tasks.title: Portfolio Product Design Case with Accessibility and Handoff
practical_tasks.brief: Create a portfolio-ready case that tells the story of a feature you designed, emphasizing accessibility improvements and an implementation-ready handoff. The case should be consumable by hiring managers and engineers.
acceptance_criteria: A written narrative (PDF or web) 800–1500 words covering problem, constraints, approach, decision points, outcomes, and reflection.
Before/after visuals: key screens and flows with callouts to specific changes and why.
A section summarizing accessibility work: issues found (mapped to WCAG), design changes, and how these were validated.

A handoff package: link to a Figma file with components, variant states, and Inspect showing token names (not just numbers) for at least buttons and form fields; include exported design tokens (JSON) or documented mapping.
Evidence of impact: at least two artifacts such as task metrics, a short clip, or an audit delta table. If metrics are inconclusive, explain confounds and show qualitative/a11y value.
A checklist for engineers in the case or Figma file outlining interaction behaviors (focus, keyboard, error states) and platform mappings (e.g., dp/pt).
All external links accessible to a reviewer without special permissions (or provide view-only access).

rubric.criterion: Narrative clarity and completeness with defensible, ethical storytelling
Before/after artifacts and callouts clearly tie design choices to problems
Accessibility section maps issues to WCAG and shows concrete fixes/validation
Handoff quality: tokens present in Inspect, component variants/states, and dev checklist
Evidence of impact or clear handling of inconclusive results
